articles.title: I built a drone with only one motor [video]
articles.summary: I built a drone with only one motor [video]

top_comments: Just want to mention that hobbyists into fixed wing RC aerobatics have been doing crazy stuff with variable pitch propellers (VPP) for several years. RC motors with integrated variable pitch propellers exist in small sizes, so no need to DIY the propeller for that application. Here's an example of the 4D aerobatics they enable: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j5EsvZNvVRs.This is similar to but different than what the creator of the one motor drone is doing since he's spinning at higher RPM with the pitch varying under CPU control much faster than fixed wing aerobatic pilots who are controlling everything manually with insane skill. I assume the one motor drone guy already knows fixed wing RC VPP exist, just mentioning for others who might not.

Underactuated robotics are so cool. In the hobby BattleBots community, there is a design where the whole robot only has a single motor, but it's able to move in any direction and damage the opponent, all just by controlling the single motor's speed.Most robots have at least three motors, two drive sides and a weapon motor. The trick to getting away with one is integrating an impactor into the chassis of your bot, using the single wheel to spin up to ~3k RPM, then by tracking the rotation angle of the bot as it spins, you speed up a little while the wheel is pointing where you want to go, and slow it down a little when it's pointing the other direction.

This is well worth the entire watch. It feels like what would any hacker do in trying to figure out how to make something they want to exist. Also very well presented and good pace.Inspires me to try and start doing some robotics.

This model seems to be pretty benchmaxed. In actual use, it doesn't survive the comparison to models in the benchmark.This model was released as a "stealth model" in OpenCode Go for a while as "Space Bunny" (they mention this in the blog). So people have been using without knowing what the model was exactly, but it failed to impress anyone as far as I can tell. This is despite the model being served for free (with some asterisks). GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, even before last week's update, seemed to be much preferred. Stealth releases happen often with OpenCode subscriptions, and GLM 5.3 Flash (stealth name "Ox Alpha") impressed a lot for example.The perverse incentives around benchmarks are now so bad that benchmark scores are effectively meaningless. Models can score highly and still be crap to use. It doesn't matter whether it's Minimax or Google, or anyone really.

In our data analytics benchmark, it got the best score of all of the Chinese models and tied Opus 5.5 & Argon (41/43 questions correct). It's also 1/3rd the price of both of those models. However, it seems to use A LOT of tokens and it's the slowest model that we've tested for the exam; it's slow because of the number of tokens it uses, not the inference speed.We also tested Space Bunny (its stealth version) a few weeks ago and the behavior changed quite a bit. Went from 30s / question to 3 minutes / question and the accuracy improved quite a bit.[1]This benchmark is short-horizon data analytics questions, so not fully representative of software engineering tasks. YMMV.[1] https://plotly.com/blog/minimax-m3-1-flash-plotly-data-analy...

I'm finding these LLM announcements to be pretty meaningless. They all look the same, with different numbers and graphs, even though the graphs are almost all identical. The offered model is compared with models that it can beat, with a couple of entries that "show" they haven't engineered the whole benchmark presentation to mislead.I've become incredibly skeptical of new model announcements until I can find evidence of someone else using it for something effective. I'd love to see an announcement that wasn't structured around attracting investors with too much money and too little domain knowledge.

top_comments: OpenBSD 7.9 was already on the 6.18.y longterm support version for the drm(4) drivers, Jonathan Gray (jsg@) completed the update back in March, sponsored by the OpenBSD Foundation.https://marc.info/?l=openbsd-cvs&m=177310343311915&w=2I just wanted to highlight Jonathan's continued efforts backporting updates in my usual "HYPE" post series for the upcoming OpenBSD 8.0 release.(I'm the author of the mastodon post that was shared.)

Note that OpenBSD is on 7.9 now and all releases are possible breaking changes.They release every six month and increment by 0.1. And after 0.9 they rollover to the next whole number.So don’t think of version “8.0” as a major release per se, since OpenBSD is a fixed schedule release - not a Major.Minor release.
How does GPL code get ported to BSD?

I have a Lenovo laptop running OpenBSD 8.0.What I really appreciate about it is I started with OpenBSD 7.6. Using sysupgrade, I went through every release (and syspatch) and just now successfully upgraded to 8.0. It still works great!
When I read the Changelog I had to check if it was April Fools day. Is this a real OpenBSD release? Feels early. Also, many of those changes don't sound like real OpenBSD changes.
